title: Uber ($Uber) Q2 2026 Update, We've Taken a Position
snippet: After a year+ on the sidelines, Casteleyn Partnership is now a shareholder
content_html:
Dear partners,

Uber released its H1 ‘26 results today. Uber’s share price is currently down 6% on the back of these results. Were these figures bad, then?

We’ll start by discussing the potential takeover of Delivery Hero, and then we’ll look at the figures

Delivery Hero (M&A)

Uber has announced that it has acquired Delivery Hero. As a result, it will enter or expand into 50 active markets, with a total GMV of $42 billion by 2025. In the competitive landscape of the food delivery market, I believe this is a good deal for Uber. I will also explain my view and the dynamics of the delivery market in a bit more detail

The only way for a company to stand out in the delivery sector, where competition is fierce, is through an extreme customer obsession. There are three focus areas for these delivery companies:

  1. - Price

  2. - ⁠Convenience + fast delivery

  3. - ⁠Selection

This relentless focus is only possible and driven by the platform with the best infrastructure, which is the with the most restaurants and delivery drivers and serving them with the best data tools. However, without scale, the Delivery business model is not profitable; margins are thin and everything hinges on achieving the right scale in the market. Here you can see the flywheel of delivery business models:

Every end market has its own dynamics, and customer loyalty in the food delivery market is also very thin. Customers will switch to another app for just a few cents, so for food delivery and mobility platforms, the key is to make their app a habit for customers and to grow organically, without having to buy $20–30 vouchers for a customer who will simply switch to another platform later on. To illustrate the types of customers in Uber’s food delivery segment:

With the acquisition of Delivery Hero, Uber does not need to try to force its way into these 50 markets by pumping huge amounts of money into the market to create scale; instead, it can further scale up Delivery Hero’s local brands and, as time goes on, gradually integrate them into the Uber brand.

Furthermore, Delivery Hero is already well advanced with Q-Commerce in its operational markets through its local Dmarts. This is an area where Uber has not yet made significant inroads, and it immediately provides infrastructure for Uber’s platform. Q-Commerce increases the range of products available on the platform, making it increasingly attractive to customers and merchant partners.

The platforms make little profit from providing these delivery services, but retailers are keen to feature prominently in the app and pay Uber a lot of money to ensure their products are highly visible within it. Advertising makes the delivery segment more profitable, and Delivery Hero in particular is very successful with advertising in its Everyday app , or so it would seem. Profitable revenue from advertising on the Delivery Hero platform accounts for 3% of total GMV, whilst for Uber this figure is still only around 1%. The overview below shows the delivery landscape as a whole, with Uber not yet very active in 1P:

A network effect of the platform, and precisely what makes Uber’s position so strong following this acquisition, is that it can immediately roll out Mobility in these markets or, conversely, give it a boost through cross-platform selling. This gives Uber a dual strategy (Delivery + Mobility) expanding from 34 to 58 markets.

Whereas a few years ago delivery platforms could raise money for free and buy their way to growth, the market has consolidated significantly in recent years. Each market now often has just three or four serious players, down from six previously. In local markets in particular, local expertise is extremely important for meeting customers’ exacting expectations. Through Delivery Hero, Uber is acquiring various local delivery platforms, many of which are market leaders. This is extremely important, as each market has its own specific characteristics in terms of customers, restaurants, delivery drivers, merchants and regulations. Uber is therefore not just buying growth, but rather infrastructure upon which it can continue to build in the coming years, without having to do so itself. Furthermore, the faster and more deeply Uber becomes embedded in customers’ minds and daily habits, the less likely it is to be disrupted in the future, given that Uber possesses the most data and the largest customer base.

This is particularly important now that Uber is playing a strategic game of chess in the field of autonomous driving. At first glance, this is an understandable strategy on the part of management. The deal’s completion in H2 2027 depends on competition and financial regulators, as well as shareholders tendering their shares. Prosus has already committed, bringing Uber’s economic interest to ~53%.

All in all, we’ll have to wait a little longer until the deal is finalised, and then we’ll look into this in more detail. Let’s now move on to today’s Q2 figures:

MAPCs

MAPCs (Monthly Active Platform Consumers) are simply the number of unique customers who take a ride or have an order delivered at least once a month. For me, this is the fuel that drives the whole flywheel. Because, without a constant stream of new and active users, the flywheel breaks. In Q2 2026, Uber recorded 208 million MAPCs, a 15,6% increase compared with the previous year (180 million).

At first glance, that growth has levelled off slightly (it was 18% in Q4 and 17% in Q1), but far more important than the figure itself is where that growth is coming from. Uber management stated that over the past twelve months it has added more new users than in any other period over the past five years. And this is despite marketing expenditure as a percentage of turnover remaining low (below 10%). That is exactly what you want to see. Customers are coming on the platform because the brand has become a habit, not because Uber has to lure them in with expensive adverts or vouchers. New customers acquired virtually for free are the most valuable customers there are.

Why is this so important for the flywheel? MAPCs form the top of the funnel and determine the size of the entire network on which the rest operates. The more customers on the platform, the more attractive the platform becomes to drivers, restaurants and merchants. Greater supply means shorter waiting times and more choice, which in turn makes the platform more attractive to the next customer.

As long as this engine continues to run on organic growth, this is, for me, the earliest indication that the moat is healthy. A structural slowdown here would be the first sign that the top of the funnel is cooling off, and that is therefore the first thing I keep an eye on every quarter.

Trips

Whilst MAPCs measure reach, Trips measure engagement on the platform – specifically, the total number of completed journeys and deliveries. And that’s a key difference, because it’s not enough just to have lots of users; you want them to actually use the platform frequently. The formula I look at is simple: MAPCs × frequency (Trips per MAPC) = Trips. In Q2 2026, no fewer than 3.9 billion trips were completed, an 18% increase on the previous year. The frequency stood at 6.2 trips per user per month (+2%).

Trips (+18%) are still growing faster than MAPCs (+16%). This is precisely the vertical growth that matters. Existing customers are using Uber more and more frequently and are therefore becoming more valuable, without Uber having to spend a single extra cent on customer acquisition.

However, growth in Trips has slowed by 2 percentage points (from +20% in Q1). According to management, this slowdown stems almost entirely from a single market; Brazil, Uber’s largest market in terms of volume. There was a temporary shortage of drivers in the cheaper Moto segment (two-wheelers), partly due to competition from delivery platforms for those same drivers. This is therefore not a demand problem but a supply problem, and Uber is already seeing a recovery in Q3. To me, this is actually a perfect illustration of how the flywheel works:

Too few drivers → longer waiting times → fewer journeys.

Looking at the incentives on the platform, a record 10.2 million drivers and couriers earned more than $25 billion on the platform this quarter. It is the supply side that must keep pace with demand, and as long as those two remain in balance, the flywheel will keep turning.

Gross Bookings

Gross Bookings are the total dollar value of all transactions on the platform. If I could choose just one KPI to track for Uber, it would be this one. Gross Bookings are the purest measure of the marketplace’s size and health, and the figure least distorted by accounting choices in a single revenue line item. The formula builds logically on the previous two sections: Trips × value per trip = Gross Bookings.

In Q2 2026, Gross Bookings reached a record $58.0 billion, representing growth of 24% (and 22% on a constant-currency basis). This meant Uber exceeded the upper end of its own guidance given, and it is now the fourth consecutive quarter of growth exceeding 20%. What I particularly like here is that the growth is extremely broad-based; it is not coming from just one segment or one region. Mobility grew by 20%, Delivery and Freight both accelerated to 25%, and both the US and international markets continued to perform strongly. The US market even accelerated, which is impressive for such a mature market, partly due to the 2026 World Cup.

Gross Bookings are the lifeblood of the marketplace. If this figure continues to compound at 20%+, whilst the price per ride remains stable and profitability increases at the same time, then you’re looking at a healthy, thriving business. And that is precisely the most difficult thing for a new entrant to replicate, as they would have to build up both the demand and supply sides simultaneously. The fact that the record of 10.2 million drivers and couriers goes hand in hand with this growth shows that both sides of the network are developing in tandem. As long as Gross Bookings maintain this pace, the rest of the business will follow.

Revenue (Take Rate)

Whilst Gross Bookings measure everything that flows through the platform, Revenue measures the portion that Uber itself retains. The take rate is the percentage of Gross Bookings that Uber retains as commission after drivers, restaurants and couriers have been paid. The formula is therefore: Gross Bookings × take rate = Revenue. For me, it is not so much the level of the take rate that matters, but rather its quality.

In Q2 2026, revenue stood at $14.2 billion, representing growth of 12% (11% on a constant-currency basis). At first glance, this represents a significant dip compared with the 22% growth in Gross Bookings, and that might give cause for concern. However, there is a purely accounting-related effect at play here that needs to be factored out: the change to the business model in the United Kingdom reduced revenue by $1.1 billion, or approximately 8 percentage points of growth. Without that UK effect, revenue would therefore have grown by around 19–20%, in line with Gross Bookings. Put simply, what is happening in the UK is that payments to drivers are being reclassified within the accounts from ‘cost of revenue’ to ‘contra-revenue’, causing both reported revenue and the take rate to appear lower. This does not alter the underlying economics in the slightest.

If you work out the take rates by segment, you can see exactly why you shouldn’t just look at the headline figure. The total take rate came in at around 24.5%. In Mobility, revenue was $7.4 billion, representing growth of just 1% (0% cc), but that growth is almost entirely down to the UK effect (accounting for around 400 bps of the mobility revenue margin), not a weakening of the business. In Delivery, revenue grew by 28% (26% cc) to $5.2 billion, outpacing Gross Bookings, which equates to a take rate of around 19% that is moving in the right direction.

Take Rate Development

I don’t mind a falling take rate in Mobility at all, and it will possibly fall further due to competition in AVs. In fact, you want to see Uber choose to pass on economies of scale to drivers and customers (lower prices, better pay); this keeps both sides of the marketplace loyal and allows you to continue driving up Gross Bookings whilst gradually expanding their AV strategy within mobility. The take rate I do want to see rise, however, is that of Delivery, and for a specific reason: advertising. Advertising revenue has a margin of almost 80-100%, so as it grows, it boosts the effective take rate without squeezing more out of the core transaction.

Mobility

As already mentioned in relation to Gross Bookings, the Mobility segment continued to grow strongly, with a 20% increase to $29 billion in Gross Bookings. Operating income stood at $2.2 billion, a 28% increase, representing a margin of 7.6% of Gross Bookings. Uber is investing heavily in improving and expanding its product mix within the Mobility segment and, through AI, is also finding that it can offer consumers better-tailored ride suggestions. This is, of course, the strength of the Uber platform; it is purely data-driven and, particularly now with AI, they can personalise that data to meet the customer’s needs. These are positive developments for the platform.

However, as investors, we must look to the future, which remains uncertain due to new technologies such as autonomous driving. Earlier this year, I wrote a 33-page analysis of the AV market:

Uber is now operating AVs in seven cities and will launch them in a further eight by the end of 2026, on its way to 15 cities. Uber has not tied itself to a single technology, but is partnering with hardware platforms (Lucid, Nissan, Verne, Volkswagen), an impressive line-up of self-driving tech companies (Waymo, Nuro, Pony.ai, WeRide, Zoox, Wayve, Baidu, Momenta, Motional, Avride) and specialist fleet management partners (Hertz, Avomo, Otto and more). Management’s view on developments in autonomous vehicles is, just as with AI, that there will not be a single winning model, but rather an entire ecosystem of players and that is precisely what makes the commercialisation layer, where Uber operates, all the more valuable.

According to management an AV partner launching with Uber achieves a utilisation rate of mid-to-high 20s to low 30s journeys per vehicle per day, thanks to Uber’s built-in demand, and that is crucial to making those expensive vehicles profitable. AVs currently account for a few hundred thousand journeys per week, whilst Uber handles around 300 million per week. AVs therefore still account for less than 0.5% of the total. It’s a marathon, not a sprint, whilst Uber will continue to benefit significantly from its market leadership in driver-operated mobility over the coming years and is also expanding into smaller suburbs. The message from management is that in the most mature AV markets (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Phoenix), Uber’s market share is now higher than it was a year ago. Hopefully, these are early signs of what we wrote in our Deep Dive: that AVs are expanding the total market rather than cannibalising Uber.

We need to keep an eye on the developmets from quarter to quarter. Perhaps a important piece of news from the last quarter: Waymo has informed Uber that, from January 2028, it will offer its robotaxis in Austin and Atlanta via its own app, once the current contract expires. Until then, hundreds of Waymo vehicles will remain available on Uber, reportedly until around May 2028 (the end of the contract term). In Phoenix, the exclusivity agreement had already ended earlier, around the end of June 2026, with Waymo’s cars now back in its own fleet and app.

Delivery

Whilst Mobility is the flagship, Delivery is, in my view, the most underrated part of Uber and the segment that delivered the strongest figures this quarter (and in recent quarters). Gross Bookings accelerated to 25% growth (on a constant-currency basis) to $27.5 billion, and revenue grew by as much as 28% to $5.2 billion. Delivery is now close to matching Mobility in size.

Segment operating income came in at $1.055 billion, a growth of no less than 38%, representing an operating margin of 3.8% of Gross Bookings (up from 3.5% a year ago and 3.7% last quarter). This is evidence of operating leverage, despite the thin margins affecting the entire food delivery industry; perhaps we can also say that Uber is not growing through a subsidy war (vouchers), which is very positive.

Advertising & Uber One

Where does this improvement in margins come from? Largely from advertising. CEO Dara said that the record margins in Delivery are mainly due to the scalability of the advertising products. The cost of displaying one extra advert is virtually zero, whilst the value for the merchant and for Uber is enormous. In addition, Uber One now accounts for more than 70% of Delivery Gross Bookings (two years ago, that figure was around 20 percentage points lower). For these members, Uber has become a habit, as they order more frequently and the churn costs associated with a subscription are also higher because these subscribers stay for longer.

G&R

In my view, the greatest opportunity for the Delivery sector lies in Grocery & Retail, as this broadens the selection for both customers and merchants. For Uber, this now amounts to $15 billion in annualised Gross Bookings and has been growing at around 40% per annum for several consecutive quarters. New partners such as Tesco, Decathlon, Ulta Beauty, GameStop are continually expanding the range on offer, and according to Uber, customers who buy groceries demonstrably remain loyal for longer than those who only order restaurant meals. Features on the platform, such as the AI-driven Cart Assistant (which generates shopping baskets that are on average twice the normal size), only reinforce this trend. Uber and its industry peers (Doordash, Delivery Hero, Didi etc.) are thus transforming from a delivery app into a broader infrastructure for local commerce.

Capital allocation

For the first time in history, free cash flow over the past twelve months exceeded $10 billion ($10.1 billion excluding SBC adjustments). Free cash flow gives management the luxury of simultaneously investing in the future, making a major acquisition and buying back shares. The CFO summed it up aptly: “we can do both.” Uber ended the quarter with $5.4 billion in freely available cash and a further ~$12.5 billion in investments (largely listed holdings) on the balance sheet.

Around 50% of free cash flow is allocated to share buy-backs. This quarter, management deliberately deviated from this approach. In Q2, Uber bought back around $510 million worth of its own shares, less than the $1.4 billion a year earlier. The reason for this was that it acquired a major stake of around $4 billion in Delivery Hero. For the year as a whole, the total for share buybacks still stands at ~$3.5 billion, and despite the slower pace this quarter, the number of outstanding shares still fell by ~4% year-on-year. There remains ~$16 billion available under the current authorisation. In the coming quarters, management will step up share buybacks again.

A commitment of over $10 billion to the AV strategy

In terms of capital allocation Uber today announced that it will commit over $10 billion to bringing AVs to market on a large scale. Firstly, it will invest in AV software partners, typically through equity stakes with clear milestones, which will give Uber insight into the roadmap and a place ‘at the front of the queue’ when it comes to commercialisation. The key benefit here is the leverage. Uber’s role as an anchor investor attracts external capital. For every dollar Uber invests, the partners themselves raise a further $2.50.

Secondly, Uber is selectively using its balance sheet to build the AV infrastructure on the ground, such as fleet operations, property and off-take commitments to manufacturers. This ties in with the ~120,000 vehicles that partners have committed to the Uber network over the coming years.

What makes this a sensible strategy, in my view, is that Uber does not have to bear the entire cost itself. Management is actively ‘financialising’ the ecosystem by attracting external financial partners to bolster Uber’s investments, thereby keeping the balance sheet flexible. Uber does not want to build the expensive hardware; it wants to be the commercialisation layer and to do so in a capital-efficient manner.

Conclusion Casteleyn Partnership

Another strong quarter for Uber, and if they continue at this rate and manage to increase their EPS, the share price will follow suit in the long run.

We can announce that we took a position in Uber last quarter and have added to that position today. I’m on holiday at the moment, but I’ll share an investment thesis with you once I’m back.

Thank you for reading!
